Courses/Bluetooth Low Energy, from the radio up

Puzzle 4 · 5 of 5

Don't ask, get told

In puzzle 3, the phone read the battery level by asking for it. A live heart rate can't work that way: asking again and again wastes radio time, and the standard doesn't even allow reading it. Here's how the strap tells the phone instead, and the one step everyone forgets.

  • Puzzle 3: The filing cabinet

    GATT organizes a device's data like a filing cabinet: services are drawers, characteristics are folders holding one value, each named by a UUID. The GATT server holds them; the GATT client reads and writes them.

    Review puzzle 3

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 4 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

In puzzle 3, the phone read the battery level by asking: "read 2A19". Imagine showing a live heart rate the same way: the phone would have to ask at every connection event. That's a request and an answer each time, even when the value didn't change, and each read waits for a meeting to ask and for the answer (puzzle 3), so the value can be old by the time it arrives. Can the strap just tell the phone when the value changes? For the heart rate, that's the only way the standard allows.

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Yes: that's a notification. The GATT server sends a characteristic's new value by itself at the next connection event, without being asked. The meetings still happen; what's saved is the request and answer packets, and the value arrives as soon as it changes.

But the strap doesn't notify everyone by default. A characteristic can carry extra settings called descriptors. Descriptors have UUIDs too, and a client can write them. One of them, the CCCD (Client Characteristic Configuration Descriptor, UUID 2902), holds a switch per client: bit 0 on means "notify me". The client turns notifications on by writing that descriptor on the device.

On Android, your app gets a BluetoothGatt object when it connects: Android's handle for that connection's GATT client. After service discovery you find the characteristic by its UUIDs. Then turning notifications on takes two separate steps: setCharacteristicNotification() on the phone, and writeDescriptor() to the strap. A short UUID like 2902 is written in full as Bluetooth's standard base number with those four digits in it, which is the long string in the code.

val characteristic = gatt.getService(HEART_RATE).getCharacteristic(MEASUREMENT)   // HEART_RATE and MEASUREMENT: your UUID constants
gatt.setCharacteristicNotification(characteristic, true)   // 1. on the phone: pass these to my app
val cccd = characteristic.getDescriptor(UUID.fromString("00002902-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb"))   // 2902, written in full
gatt.writeDescriptor(cccd, BluetoothGattDescriptor.ENABLE_NOTIFICATION_VALUE)   // 2. on the strap: bit 0 on

setCharacteristicNotification() only tells your own phone to hand this characteristic's notifications to your app. It sends nothing to the strap. writeDescriptor() is what flips the switch on the strap. Skip it, and the strap never sends a thing: the classic "connected, but no data" bug.

The analogy

Instead of phoning the newsroom every hour to ask "anything new?", you subscribe. But the subscription has two halves: you tell your own mailbox to accept the paper, and you send the form to the newspaper. Do only the first, and your mailbox waits forever.

Check yourself

Your app calls setCharacteristicNotification(characteristic, true) and nothing else. The heart rate changes. What arrives?

Not quite. No notifications are sent at all until the CCCD is written.

Not quite. That call only prepares your own phone. The strap starts sending only when its CCCD is written.

Right. Two steps: your phone, and the switch on the strap.

Why are notifications cheaper than reading again and again?

Not quite. They still travel at connection events; the saving is the request and answer packets, and fresher values.

Right. No request, and nothing sent when nothing changed.

Not quite. Same value, same bytes; the saving is not having to ask.

What's the difference between a characteristic and a descriptor?

Not quite. It's not the value: it describes or configures the characteristic.

Right. Value vs a setting about that value.

Sources
  • Bluetooth Core Specification 5.4, Vol 3, Part G: GATT (Client Characteristic Configuration: "Bit 0: Notification. The Characteristic Value shall be notified"; the descriptor value is kept per client)
  • Bluetooth SIG assigned numbers: descriptors (0x2902: Client Characteristic Configuration)
  • Android Developers: Transfer BLE data (the sample calls setCharacteristicNotification() and then writes the descriptor with ENABLE_NOTIFICATION_VALUE)
  • Bluetooth SIG: Heart Rate Service 1.0 (characteristic table: "Heart Rate Measurement / M / Notify / None", no Read property)

What you now know

A notification is the server sending a characteristic's value by itself when it changes. It only starts after the client writes the CCCD descriptor on the device. On Android, setCharacteristicNotification() alone isn't enough: you also writeDescriptor() the CCCD.
